knowledge: A regular chat is the default: one conversation for a one-off question, draft or quick analysis. Separate chats do not share context with each other.
A Project is a self-contained workspace with its own chat history, knowledge files and instructions; its knowledge and instructions apply to every chat inside it.

Web search finds up-to-date information and cites its sources. Research goes further: it runs many searches that build on each other, can include connected tools, and produces an in-depth, cited report, but takes longer and uses your allowance faster.
An artifact is substantial, self-contained output, such as a document, deck, dashboard or small interactive tool, that opens beside the chat and can be edited, revisited and shared.
Features combine: you can run Research inside a Project, and ask for an artifact in any chat or Project.
Artifacts and skills rely on code execution and file creation being turned on; on work plans an admin may control this.
skills: Match the feature to the shape of the work: one-off, recurring with shared context, deep multi-source investigation, or a deliverable to reuse.
Choose web search for a quick current fact and Research for a multi-source, cited report.
Set up a Project when the same files and guidance would otherwise be pasted into every new chat.
Ask for an artifact when the output will be edited, shared or reused outside the conversation.
examLens: "Uploads the same files every week" points to a Project.
"Comprehensive, cited overview from many sources" points to Research; "one current figure or headline" points to web search.
"Something the team will keep editing or share" points to an artifact.
traps: Using Research for a simple lookup or a rewording task; it is slower and uses more of your allowance.
Assuming separate chats share context; only Project knowledge (or memory) carries across.
Re-uploading the same reference files into every new chat instead of creating a Project.

columns.head: Research
items: Many searches that build on each other

knowledge: Claude comes in model tiers; the exam blueprint names three: Haiku, Sonnet and Opus.
Haiku is the fastest, lowest-cost tier, built for high-volume, straightforward work such as sorting, tagging and pulling out key details.
Sonnet balances speed and intelligence and suits most everyday work, such as drafting content and analysing data.
Opus is the most capable of the three, for complex, multi-step reasoning and demanding knowledge work; it is slower and uses more of your allowance.
The model menu lets you change the model (and effort and thinking) mid-chat; the change applies from the next response.
Exact versions and which models appear in the menu change over time, and an admin may limit them, so learn the tiers by position, not by version number.
skills: Describe each tier by its relative speed, cost and capability.
Read task signals: volume and simplicity suit Haiku, everyday balance suits Sonnet, depth and complexity suit Opus.
Explain to a colleague why a bigger model is not automatically better for every task.
examLens: Questions describe tiers by position (fastest and lowest cost vs most capable), not by version.
"High volume, simple, speed matters" means Haiku; "everyday mix" means Sonnet; "complex, high-stakes reasoning" means Opus.
traps: Assuming the most capable model is always the best choice.
Assuming the fastest model can handle deep, multi-step analysis just because it answers quickly.
Memorising version numbers; they change, and the tier is what matters.

knowledge: Choosing a model balances three things: quality (capability), speed and cost, including how quickly you use your plan's allowance.
Two sound strategies: start with a smaller, faster model and move up only where it falls short, or start with the most capable and step down once you know the quality you need.
Test the choice on your real tasks and examples rather than guessing.
Effort is a separate lever: higher effort gives more thorough answers but is slower and uses more; adjusting effort is often better than switching models.
Usage also grows with long conversations, large attachments, Research and web search, not only with the model.
On work plans an admin may limit which models or effort levels are available.
skills: Identify the requirement that dominates: volume and speed, everyday balance, or depth and accuracy.
Split a mixed workflow: a fast tier for bulk steps and a capable tier for the hard, high-stakes step.
Adjust effort or thinking before, or alongside, switching models.
Run a small trial on real examples and compare quality before committing.
examLens: Look for the dominant constraint: "high volume", "quickly", "budget" versus "complex", "nuanced", "high-stakes".
The best answer matches tier to task and reserves the most capable model for the work that needs it.
Quality falling short on a smaller model is fixed by moving up a tier or raising effort, not by abandoning the task.
traps: Using the top model at maximum effort for everything "to be safe"; it wastes time and allowance.
Choosing the cheapest model for high-stakes analysis because of cost alone.
Switching platforms or turning off features to save cost instead of matching the model to the task.

knowledge: The context window is Claude's working memory for a single chat; it holds the conversation and attached files, and its size depends on the model.

Long chats use more of your allowance with each message; when a chat nears its limit Claude can automatically summarise earlier messages and carry on (where code execution is on), but very long chats can still hit limits.
Start a new chat for a new topic, or when a long chat nears its limits, bringing a short summary of decisions so far.
Chats don't share context. Persist anything future chats need in a Project's knowledge or instructions, or in memory.
Memory saves topics as you chat; you can ask Claude to remember, change or forget something, and view or edit memory topics. Each Project keeps its own memory.
Deleting a chat does not remove memories made from it. Incognito chats are not saved to history or memory and do not use existing memory.
skills: Decide whether to continue, restart with a summary, or persist information into a Project or memory.
Ask Claude for a handover summary of decisions, open questions and next steps before starting fresh.
Move reference material every chat needs into Project knowledge instead of pasting it repeatedly.
Keep one topic per chat and batch related questions into one message.

"Needed in every future chat" means persist: Project knowledge, instructions or memory.
"Sensitive one-off that shouldn't be remembered" means an incognito chat, within policy.
traps: Running one endless chat for every topic.
Expecting a new chat to know what an earlier chat concluded without adding it to Project knowledge.
Deleting a chat to remove something from memory; the memory topic must be edited or deleted itself.

columns.head: Project knowledge
items: Used in every chat of the Project

knowledge: A Project has two main settings: instructions (how Claude should work in every chat here) and knowledge (files and text Claude uses as context in every chat here).
Claude cannot see the Project's name or description, so anything it needs must go into the instructions or knowledge.
Project instructions suit project-specific context: role or perspective, audience, workflow steps, output requirements and tone.

When knowledge grows large, paid plans switch automatically to a retrieval mode that pulls only the relevant parts; clear file names, related content kept together and naming the document in your question all help.
On Team and Enterprise plans a Project can be shared as Can view (use it and chat) or Can edit (change instructions, knowledge and members).
Each Project has its own memory, kept separate from other Projects.
skills: Turn a recurring task into a Project: define its purpose, write instructions, upload the reference files.
Write instructions that cover role, audience, format and boundaries in short, specific statements.
Name and organise knowledge files so the right one is easy to find.
Set sharing permissions: Can view for users, Can edit only for maintainers.
examLens: "How Claude should behave" goes in instructions; "what Claude should know" goes in knowledge.
Guidance written only in the project name or description is invisible to Claude.
Before rolling a Project out, test it with real requests.
traps: Putting key guidance in the project description, which Claude never sees.
Uploading everything "just in case"; unrelated or outdated files dilute answers and use more allowance.
Giving every user Can edit, so instructions drift.

knowledge: An uploaded file is a snapshot: it stays as uploaded until someone replaces it.
Connectors link Claude to apps such as Google Drive, Gmail and Google Calendar so it can search, read and, with your approval, take actions; answers cite the emails, documents or events used.
Claude inherits your permissions: it can only reach what your own account can reach in the connected app.
Connecting a service lets Claude access and potentially change data there, so connect only services you trust and need, and turn off connectors a chat doesn't need.
Google Docs added through the Drive connector stay synced to the latest version. The Gmail connector sees attachment details but not attachment contents.
On Team and Enterprise plans an owner enables each connector for the organisation, and each person still signs in individually; custom connectors are added by owners and are a technical job.
skills: Choose upload or connector: stable reference material is uploaded; a living document comes through the Drive connector.
Review approval requests before Claude sends, changes or deletes anything.
Limit scope: share only the files and services the work needs, especially where data is sensitive.
Escalate requests for a new or custom connector to an admin or a Claude Developer or Architect.
examLens: "The file keeps changing and answers go stale" points to the Drive connector instead of re-uploading.
"Connect everything just in case" is wrong; least access and only trusted services is right.
A tool with no connector is an escalation, not a do-it-yourself integration.
traps: Connecting broad accounts full of sensitive data that the task doesn't need.
Assuming an owner enabling a connector signs everyone in, or that Claude can see more than you can.
Approving actions such as sending an email without reading the draft and recipients.
Expecting an uploaded file to update itself when the original changes.

knowledge: Standing instructions apply automatically so you don't repeat them: Instructions for Claude cover all your chats, project instructions cover one Project's chats, and on Team and Enterprise plans organization instructions set by owners cover everyone.
Organization instructions take precedence over individual instructions when they conflict.
Skills package a repeatable procedure or house style and load only when relevant; instructions apply to every chat in their scope. Anthropic now recommends skills for consistent tone and format.
Good instructions are concise (they are read with every message), specific ("formal English, no contractions" rather than "be professional"), consistent and free of contradictions.
Explaining why a rule matters, and giving a short example, helps Claude apply it well.
Instructions cannot override Claude's safety behaviour or your organisation's policies.
skills: Put each instruction at the right level: personal, project or organisation.
Rewrite vague rules into concrete, checkable ones.
Remove contradictions and duplicates across levels.
Test new instructions on typical requests before relying on them.
examLens: "Outputs vary" with adjectives like "professional" or "short" means make the rule specific and measurable.
A rule for one client or team belongs in that Project, not in account-wide instructions.
A conflict between organisation and personal instructions is resolved in favour of the organisation.
traps: Vague adjectives with no concrete standard.
Putting project-specific rules into account-wide instructions, where they leak into every chat.
Long, contradictory rule lists, or trying to instruct Claude past safety behaviour.

knowledge: Configurations go stale: policies, prices, product details and processes change, and Claude can only use the version of a file it has.
Replace outdated files instead of adding a new version beside the old one; conflicting versions produce inconsistent answers.
Remove unused files and keep instructions short; a lean configuration focuses answers and saves allowance.
Give each shared Project an owner and a review rhythm; only people with Can edit can change its instructions and knowledge.
Tell users when a shared Project's instructions or knowledge change, and retest with typical requests after each change.
Review memory too: edit or delete outdated memory topics, or ask Claude to forget them. Turn off connectors the work no longer needs.
skills: Run a periodic review of files, instructions and connectors against current sources.
Retest with a small set of standard requests after every change.
Keep a short change note: what changed, when and by whom.
Fix the root cause: if answers cite an old policy, replace the file instead of correcting each chat.
examLens: "Answers mix old and new figures" means an outdated file is still in knowledge: remove it.
"Correcting Claude in every chat" is a symptom; the fix is in the Project's knowledge or instructions.
Changes to a shared Project are tested and announced, not made silently.
traps: Uploading a new version without removing the old one.
Correcting Claude chat by chat instead of fixing the Project.
Changing a shared Project's instructions without testing or telling its users.
Leaving unused files and connectors in place.
